c: Angels
Throughout the Bible, angels are God’s heavenly agents who carry out his purpose and communicate God’s will to humanity (
). The only angels named in the Bible are Michael and Gabriel, who carry out special assignments (
). Angels had a role in putting God’s law into effect through Moses (
). Angels dispense God’s grace and sometimes administer his judgment (
). Angels were witnesses of Christ’s life (
), and they are now witnesses of the lives of God’s people (see
). There are guardian angels who protect God’s people (
; see also
). They are “spirits sent to care for people who will inherit salvation” (
). Angels will accompany Christ when he returns (
) and will participate in the final judgment (
Angels appear at some significant points in the Gospels. Angels announced the births of John the Baptist and Jesus (
) and ministered to Jesus after his temptation (
). Angels also appeared at the empty tomb after the resurrection of Jesus (
The ministry of angels is also prominent in the book of Acts. On multiple occasions, an angel of the Lord made possible miraculous escapes from prison (
). An angel offered a message of encouragement to Paul in the midst of a violent storm (
). An angel also directed Cornelius to seek the Good News from Peter (
). Meanwhile, an angel struck down Herod Agrippa “because he accepted the people’s worship instead of giving the glory to God” (
). Throughout Acts, God was guiding his people in their ministry and using angels to accomplish his purposes.
Some angels have fallen into sin and are destined for eternal judgment (
). And although angels are spiritual and heavenly beings, angels are not to be worshiped (
) because they are inferior to Christ (
). Their role is to be servants of God (

The success of the apostles’ ministry again aroused strong opposition (cp.

Sadducees

controlled the Temple establishment and had a Temple police force at their disposal. They opposed belief in the resurrection and were determined not to allow the apostles to proclaim their message about the resurrection of Jesus unchallenged. They also sensed that their hold on the Jewish people was loosening, so,
filled with jealousy
they attacked the apostles.
The irony here is that the Sadducees denied the existence of angels (
